# Selection models

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(rnetis)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)
```

A Selection model asks what predicts a tie. `fit_selection()` fits an additive
and multiplicative effects model (Hoff 2005, 2021) through `amen::ame()`. **No
model below is fitted when this vignette is built**, because each fit is a Markov
chain that takes longer than a vignette build should. The code that builds data
and the refusals do run.

## Specify a model

Every predictor names its role, and a bare covariate is an error.

* `sender(tenure)`: does a longer-tenured actor send more ties?
* `receiver(tenure)`: does one receive more?
* `dyad(same_unit)`: a property of the pair, held as a tie variable.
* `prior_tie()`: did the relation exist at the previous wave?

`demo_selection` has one node variable and one relation, so this adds a pair
attribute for `dyad()` to read:

```{r eval = TRUE}
nodes <- netis_nodes(demo_selection)
ties <- netis_ties(demo_selection)
unit <- rep(c("u1", "u2"), length.out = nrow(nodes))
names(unit) <- nodes$node
ties$same_unit <- as.numeric(unit[ties$source] == unit[ties$target])
staff <- netis_data(nodes, ties, wave_col = "wave", tie_meta = list(
  tie = list(zero_meaning = "measured_zero"),
  same_unit = list(zero_meaning = "measured_zero")
))
```

```{r}
fit <- fit_selection(
  tie ~ sender(tenure) + receiver(tenure) + dyad(same_unit) + prior_tie(),
  data = staff,
  nscan = 5000, burn = 1000, odens = 10, seed = 1
)
summary(fit)
netis_diagnostics(fit)
```

A term read at the outcome wave is fitted and recorded with a design warning,
which `netis_diagnostics()` lists. `lag = 1` reads the previous wave instead.

## What two waves mean

`prior_tie()` uses the earlier wave as an initial condition, so two waves give
one modeled outcome:

```{r}
fit$waves$initial_waves
fit$waves$outcome_waves
```

Without a lagged relation term both waves would supply an outcome, treating
repeated observations of the same actors as independent. That is refused:

```{r eval = TRUE, error = TRUE}
fit_selection(tie ~ sender(tenure), data = demo_selection,
              nscan = 50, burn = 10)
```

With more than two waves, `waves = c(from, to)` names the transition.

## Effect sizes

A probit coefficient is not a magnitude anyone can read directly.
`selection_effect()` converts one to a contrast in predicted tie probability:

```{r}
selection_effect(fit, "prior_tie")
selection_effect(fit, "snd_tenure", delta = 1, type = "population")
```

A binary term is compared as presence against absence, and a continuous one moves
each dyad from its observed value by `delta`. `type` chooses the dyad:

* `"conditional"` averages over the observed dyads, with each actor's effect at
  its fitted value. The interval reflects uncertainty in the coefficients only.
* `"population"` is a randomly drawn dyad, integrated over the actor effects.
* `"reference"` is a hypothetical pair with actor effects at zero.

`pseudo_r2()` reports explained variation; read `?pseudo_r2` before quoting it.

## Several groups

With several groups, each is fitted on its own and the coefficients are then
combined by inverse-variance weighting (Cochran 1954; Hedges & Olkin 1985).

```{r eval = TRUE}
two_groups <- netis_data(
  node_data = rbind(transform(netis_nodes(demo_selection), group = "a"),
                    transform(netis_nodes(demo_selection), group = "b")),
  tie_data = rbind(transform(netis_ties(demo_selection), group = "a"),
                   transform(netis_ties(demo_selection), group = "b")),
  group_data = data.frame(group = c("a", "b"), size = c(8, 30)),
  wave_col = "wave",
  tie_meta = list(tie = list(zero_meaning = "measured_zero"))
)
```

```{r}
pooled <- fit_selection(tie ~ sender(tenure) + prior_tie(), data = two_groups,
                        nscan = 5000, burn = 1000, odens = 10, seed = 1)
summary(pooled)
selection_effect(pooled, "prior_tie", group = "a")

separate <- fit_selection(tie ~ sender(tenure) + prior_tie(), data = two_groups,
                          pool_beta = FALSE, nscan = 5000, burn = 1000, odens = 10, seed = 1)
coef(separate)
```

Pooling assumes a coefficient means the same thing in every group, so
between-group differences are assumed away, not estimated. It works one
coefficient at a time, so `vcov(pooled)` is an error and a contrast between
coefficients is not available. `pool_beta = FALSE` leaves the groups separate,
and `coef()` then returns one row per group.

A group-level predictor is refused, because it is collinear with the intercept
within every group:

```{r eval = TRUE, error = TRUE}
fit_selection(tie ~ group(size) + prior_tie(), data = two_groups)
```

## A hierarchical model

`pooling = selection_pooling()` fits one model over every group in one Markov
chain. A coefficient you name in `random` gets a value for each group, drawn from
a between-group distribution, and a group-level predictor enters as a moderator
of those coefficients. The model is this package's own construction from
published components; `?hierarchical_selection` specifies it.

These twelve simulated teams differ in baseline and in sender slope:

```{r eval = TRUE}
set.seed(42)
teams <- sprintf("t%02d", 1:12)
team_nodes <- do.call(rbind, lapply(teams, function(g) {
  data.frame(group = g, node = sprintf("%s_%d", g, 1:8), wave = rep(1:2, each = 8),
             extraversion = rep(stats::rnorm(8), 2))
}))
team_ties <- do.call(rbind, lapply(teams, function(g) {
  ids <- sprintf("%s_%d", g, 1:8)
  x <- team_nodes$extraversion[team_nodes$group == g & team_nodes$wave == 1]
  p <- expand.grid(source = ids, target = ids, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  p <- p[p$source != p$target, ]
  eta <- stats::rnorm(1, -0.6, 0.4) + stats::rnorm(1, 0.4, 0.25) * x[match(p$source, ids)]
  do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(w) {
    data.frame(group = g, p, wave = w, tie = stats::rbinom(nrow(p), 1, stats::pnorm(eta)))
  }))
}))
teams_data <- netis_data(team_nodes, team_ties, wave_col = "wave",
                         tie_meta = list(tie = list(zero_meaning = "measured_zero")))
```

```{r}
hier <- fit_selection(
  tie ~ sender(extraversion) + prior_tie(), data = teams_data,
  pooling = selection_pooling(random = c("intercept", "snd_extraversion")),
  nscan = 10000, burn = 1000, odens = 10, chains = 2
)
netis_hierarchy(hier)$population
```

`population` gives the mean `mu` and the between-group SD `tau` of each random
coefficient. `groups` gives each team's own values, and `convergence` gives R-hat
and effective sample sizes. Run two or more chains:
later chains start from dispersed values, so R-hat compares chains that began
apart. `?selection_pooling` covers moderators, correlated random effects and the
prior on `tau`.

## References

Cochran, W. G. (1954) The combination of estimates from different experiments.
*Biometrics* **10**(1), 101–129.

Hedges, L. V. and Olkin, I. (1985) *Statistical Methods for Meta-Analysis*.
Academic Press.

Hoff, P. D. (2005) Bilinear mixed-effects models for dyadic data. *JASA*
**100**(469), 286–295.

Hoff, P. D. (2021) Additive and multiplicative effects network models.
*Statistical Science* **36**(1), 34–50.
